text: Learning which objects may safely contact each other.
Sharpen knives using a whetstone or pull-through sharpener.
Administer pet medication (e.g., hiding a pill in a treat, dropping liquid into a water bowl).
Sick-day care: take a temperature, bring fluids, tissues, and a heating pad, clean up after vomiting, fetch an inhaler or EpiPen, bring medication on the person's own schedule and log it.

Kids: bedtime routine (bath-water temperature check, pajamas, story, night light, checking on a sleeping child), bottle and formula prep, sterilizing, supervised play (catch, hide-and-seek, card and board games), reading aloud.

Primitives: communication is thin (you have Report, Alert, and Ask for clarification). Add Speak, Listen, Announce, Explain, Confirm, Refuse, Undo, Hand off to a human, Remember, Forget. Physical verbs also missing: Cut/Slice, Peel, Crack, Tear, Hammer, Drill, Climb, Kneel/Crouch, Balance, Throw/Catch, Point/Gesture, Spray, Brush.
Pests: remove insects and spiders, clean ant trails, set and check traps, report droppings or nests, empty standing water, pantry-moth and fruit-fly traps.

Away mode. Your departure routine covers daily exits. Add a vacation or house-sitting mode: arm the alarm, set lights on timers, bring in mail and packages, water plants, check for leaks and pests, run taps, check the freezer after an outage, care for pets, send status photos.

Pets beyond feeding and walking. Give owner-directed medication, bathe and dry a dog, check for ticks and fleas, open and close crates, keep pets' meals separate, calm a pet during storms or fireworks. Aquarium water changes, filter, and glass, small-animal cages, and backyard chickens (eggs, coop, water) are also missing.
“Deal with this mess.” It has to inspect the situation and create its own cleanup plan.
“Set this room up for a party.” Number of guests, seating, food locations, walking paths, decorations, trash locations, and breakable objects all matter.
“Do the important stuff first.” Requires ranking chores by urgency and impact.
“Finish whatever I forgot to do.” It needs to inspect the environment and infer incomplete chores.
“Check whether I left anything out.” Requires understanding what the expected household state normally looks like.
“Get the house ready for the morning.” It might prepare coffee equipment, bags, clothes, lunch items, blinds, and room temperature.
“Unload the car and put everything away.” It has to classify items and route them to different locations.
“Reorganize this cabinet so everything fits better.” Requires 3D planning and category reasoning.
“Cook this without using the oven because it’s broken.” Requires replanning using different appliances.
“Finish cooking this for me.” The robot has to infer what stage the human reached.
“Watch this while it cooks.” It has to understand visual, temperature, smell, texture, and timing cues rather than just a timer.
“Take it off when it looks done.” “Done” is a perception and judgment problem.
“Use whichever pan makes sense.” The robot must select a tool from available options.
“Grab something I can use as a bowl.” Requires functional substitution rather than object-label matching.
“Move everything off this table except what we still need.” Requires understanding the current activity.
“Find where that smell is coming from.” Requires active investigation across rooms and possible causes.
“Get the usual.” Requires learning routines and preferences.
“This lid doesn’t fit. Find the right one.” Requires shape matching among similar objects.
“Make this safe for the dog.” Requires pet-specific hazard reasoning.
“Put the things we use most somewhere convenient.” Requires frequency-of-use memory.
“Open this carbonated drink without it exploding.” Requires force control, auditory/tactile feedback to detect pressure release, and pacing.
“Can this go in the microwave / dishwasher / dryer?” Requires reasoning about materials, labels, and safety.
“I’ve had a rough day.” Requires choosing between quiet, dinner, tea, or leaving them alone.
“Keep the meat and dairy dishes separate.” / “Shoes stay off.” / “Don’t touch Grandpa’s chair.” Requires picking up household rules, including cultural or sentimental ones that look arbitrary.
“Don’t buy anything; use what we have.” Requires substitution under resource limits.
